Every Sunday lunch in their north London flat, Zeynep heard a new version of the same story from her sister-in-law, Esther. The bakery on the high street had lost money for fourteen months. Esther had put in her savings, then a loan, then sold her car.

"It's turning," Esther said this Sunday, tearing bread. "The new sourdough will change everything. Anyone who quits now is weak."

Esther dried the same plate for a long time. "If it's just looking," she said. "Not quitting."
"Just looking," Zeynep said.

Francis, you asked on your show for a moment that changed me. Okay. I'm Shalini, I run a small printing business in Coimbatore, and for three years I insisted on using the same paper supplier, Mr Pillai's firm. My father had used them. qa.a: Shalini named the error, explained the real reason, loyalty, and stated a clear change: testing two other suppliers.

qa.a: Kavi likely feels respected and relieved that the evidence was heard, not argued away.

grounding: Spoken on a show, a business owner describes admitting a long-defended supplier choice was wrong and saying what would change.

I'm Tenzin, and I've worked with Chetan at the school for four years. For all that time he insisted on one thing: Class 8 homework every single night. When parents complained, he'd say, "Discipline builds character." When the counsellor raised stress, he'd list toppers who did homework daily.

Last month the school ran a survey. Chetan read it in the staff room, very slowly. Most students said they slept after midnight. His class's marks hadn't improved in three years.

I expected him to find a reason. Instead, at the next staff meeting, he stood up and said, "I was wrong about daily homework. The survey shows it. From next term my class gets three evenings a week, and one project instead." Someone clapped, awkwardly.

I don't know what it cost him inside. He went a bit red. But he looked lighter afterwards, and the Class 8 children definitely do.

qa.q: What made Chetan's statement a real correction?
qa.a: He named the mistake plainly, pointed to the evidence, and stated a specific change for next term.

grounding: A colleague describes a teacher who, faced with a survey, publicly admits a long-held homework rule was wrong and changes it.

Class teacher's note, Class 5B, 14 February.

Today Sunita's new pencil case went missing after lunch. It was found in Ritu's bag. When I asked Ritu, she said at once, "I was just borrowing it, ma'am. I was going to give it back." She had not asked Sunita, and she had moved the pencils into her own box.

This is the second time this term. The first time, she called it "keeping it safe".

I noticed how the soft words made it sound small to her. I said, "Borrowing is when someone says yes. This was taking." Ritu went red and cried a little.

We agreed she will return the case and apologise to Sunita tomorrow, and I will call her mother this evening so we can talk about it together, gently.

Disha

qa.q: Where was Sunita's pencil case found?
qa.a: The pencil case was found in Ritu's bag.

qa.q: Why did Ritu call it "just borrowing"?
qa.a: Ritu felt guilty and embarrassed, and the soft word made taking the case feel small and less like her own choice.

qa.q: What did Disha say that helped Ritu see the act clearly?
qa.a: "Borrowing is when someone says yes. This was taking." It replaced the soft word with an honest one.

qa.q: How might Sunita have felt when her pencil case went missing?
qa.a: Sunita probably felt upset and worried about her new case, and confused when it turned up emptied.

grounding: A teacher's note records a girl who calls taking a classmate's pencil case "just borrowing", and the honest word that followed.

In the village near Sangrur, Gurleen took Hansa's cycle from outside the gurdwara and rode it round the fields for an hour. When she brought it back, Hansa was crying by the gate.

"I was just borrowing it," Gurleen said, surprised. "I brought it back, na?"
"You didn't ask!" Hansa sobbed. "I thought someone stole it. I have to take milk to Nani's."

Gurleen's Dadi had seen everything from the courtyard. She came out and knelt by both girls. "Gurleen, when you borrow, what do you say first?"
Gurleen looked at the ground. "May I."
"Did you say it?"
"...No."
"Then it wasn't borrowing, puttar. It was taking, and bringing back." Dadi's voice was gentle. "Hansa was frightened for an hour."
Gurleen's face crumpled. "Sorry, Hansa. I'll help carry the milk."

qa.a: Gurleen felt it was harmless because she brought it back, and the soft word hid that she hadn't asked and had frightened Hansa.

qa.a: She asked what you say first when borrowing, named it as taking, and pointed out that Hansa had been frightened for an hour.

qa.a: Hansa was frightened and upset, thinking her cycle had been stolen when she needed it to take milk to Nani's.

At the higher secondary school in Mapusa, Francis had a routine. Every morning when Aadhya walked into class in her cousin's old uniform, he called, "Here comes the village queen!" and his friends laughed. Some days he added comments about her shoes or her English. When she didn't smile, he said, "Relax, it's banter. Everyone jokes like this."

It had gone on for six weeks. Aadhya had started slipping in just after the bell.

"Banter is when both people are laughing," Mrs Fernandes said. "She stopped laughing weeks ago, if she ever did. It stops today."

Francis opened his mouth, then closed it. He thought of Aadhya slipping in after the bell, and for the first time he didn't know what to say.

qa.a: Calling it banter let Francis feel it was harmless fun, hiding how hurt and humiliated Aadhya felt.

qa.a: She told Francis how Aadhya was affected, said banter needs both people laughing, and stopped it immediately.
